newsitem.title: CANADA: Air Canada posts disappointing 1996 results.
newsitem.headline: Air Canada posts disappointing 1996 results.

text.p: Air Canada reported on Friday a slightly higher loss in its latest quarter, capping a disappointing year in which profits were well below company forecasts.

The Montreal-based airline had a fourth-quarter loss of C$18 million ($13.3 million), or C14 cents (10 cents) a share, compared with a loss of C$12 million ($9 million) or C10 cents (seven cents) a share in the year-earlier quarter. Revenues were C$1.2 billion ($888 million) vs. C$1.1 billion ($814 million) a year earlier.

For the year, Air Canada reported a net profit of C$149 million ($110 million), or C82 cents (61 cents) a share, compared with C$62 million ($46 million) or C36 cents (27 cents) a share in 1995. Revenues were C$4.0 billion ($3.6 billion) in 1996 vs. C$4.5 billion ($3.3 billion).

Air Canada's 1996 profit was largely the result of a gain of C$129 million ($95 million) on the sale of part of its stake in Continental Airlines Corp. In 1995, it had a gain of C$57 million ($42 million) on the sale of Continental shares.
Air Canada sold the balance of its Continental stake last month.

Last February, former airline Chairman Hollis Harris had forecast that Air Canada would earn a 1996 net profit of more than C$100 million ($74 million), before any special gains like the Continental share sale.

Harris had also expected Air Canada's operating profit to surge above C$300 million ($222 million) in 1996 from C$275 million ($203 million) in 1995, but it actually fell to C$215 million ($159 million).
In a telephone conference call with reporters on Friday, company President Lamar Durrett said the 1996 results were disappointing. He said he expected higher operating profit in 1997.

Unlike Harris, who retired in August, Durrett said he would not be making any specific profit forecasts. He said 1997 revenues will be driven mainly by Air Canada's international routes, which for the first time last year accounted for more than half of the airline's ticket sales.
Durrett said the Canadian domestic market will remain tough in 1997, even though rival Canadian Airlines Corp. of Calgary is struggling with financial difficulties.
"We anticipate that the Canadian domestic market will continue to be an extremely combative area to deal in," Durrett said.
